titleText.es: Tristemente, esto es una historia real. Al menos aprendí el comando 'say' de OS X.
titleText.en: Sadly, this is a true story.  At least I learned about the OS X 'say' command.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: may I; can I (asking permission)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Puedo is the form of poder for the speaker. In a question, it can ask whether an action is allowed rather than whether the speaker is capable of doing it.

example.en: May I use the bathroom?

cardDefinitions.answerEn: female roommate; female flatmate (in compañera de piso)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Compañera can mean a female companion or colleague. With de piso, it conventionally names a female person who shares the same apartment.

example.es: Mi compañera de piso cocina muy bien.
example.en: My roommate cooks very well.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: opens; lets someone in (special form for an attempted or desired action)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Abra is a special form of abrir used when the opening is being attempted, wanted, allowed, or otherwise not stated as a fact. Compare ordinary ella abre, “she opens,” with intento que ella abra, “I try to get her to open.”

example.es: Espero que Luis abra la puerta.
example.en: I hope Luis opens the door.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: I tried
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Intenté is the completed-past form of intentar for the speaker.

example.en: I tried to call yesterday.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to call her; to phone her
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Llamar is the unchanged dictionary form meaning “to call,” and la is attached to its end for a female person receiving the call.

example.en: I am going to call her this afternoon.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: on the; a + el before the phone being called
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Al combines a and el. With llamar, Spanish can use it before the phone or number where a person is being contacted; natural English often says “on.”

example.en: I called him on his cell phone.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: off; switched off (masculine singular)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Apagado describes a masculine singular device that is not operating. The ending changes to apagada for a feminine singular thing.

example.en: The phone is switched off.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: online; connected (feminine singular)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Conectada describes a female person or feminine thing that has a network connection. The -a ending matches that feminine referent.

example.en: Marta is online now.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word here; article before a masculine technical name
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish can keep el before the name of a masculine service, protocol, or technical system even when English uses the name by itself.

example.en: Wi-Fi stopped working.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to throw something at someone's property; le marks the affected owner
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Tirar is the unchanged action form, and le attaches to its end for the person affected. Spanish can then use an ordinary article before that person's item, where natural English often uses “her” or “his.”

example.es: A Ana le tiraron pintura a la puerta.
example.en: Someone threw paint at Ana's door.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: at; toward (introducing what something is thrown at)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: After tirar or tirarle, a can introduce the person or thing used as the target.

example.es: Tiraron una pelota a la pared.
example.en: They threw a ball at the wall.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: window
the; English often uses a possessive because le already marks the affected owner
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish can use le for the affected owner and an ordinary article before that person's item. La matches a feminine singular item, not the owner's gender; natural English often uses “her” or “his” instead.

example.es: Le cerraron la cuenta a Marta.
example.en: They closed Marta's account.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: I connected; I logged in
cardDefinitions.noteEn: With me before it, conecté is the completed-past form of conectarse for the speaker: me conecté means “I connected” or “I logged in.”

example.en: I connected to the server.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: in the; de + el identifying something by its location
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Del combines de and el. After an object, it can identify which one by naming the room or place associated with it, where natural English often says “in” or puts the location before the object name.

example.en: We use the table on the patio.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: living room; lounge
to tell it to her
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Decir is the unchanged action form. In this sense, se stands for “to her,” and lo stands for the thing told. Both attach to the end, and the written accent keeps the original stress. In another context, se could instead refer to him, formal you, or them.

example.en: I have to tell it to her tomorrow.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: ended up; remained (completed form of quedarse)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Quedado is used with a form of haber to place quedarse in a completed time. A following word can name the resulting state or place.

example.en: I have ended up alone.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: volume; sound level
low (a level or setting)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Here bajo is a describing word for a masculine singular level or setting. It is different from bajo meaning “under” and from bajo meaning “I lower.”

example.en: The brightness is very low.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; presents the reading as working through a specified text
cardDefinitions.noteEn: With leer, me can add the sense that the speaker works through the stated text. It does not mean the speaker reads themself. The same completion pattern uses te, se, nos, os, or se for other people.

example.en: I read through the report last night.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: reading
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Leyendo is leer in its ongoing-action form ending in -iendo.

example.en: I am reading a book.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: documentation; technical instructions
line; part of línea de comandos (“command line”)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In computing, línea de comandos names a text interface where a person types instructions for the computer.

example.es: Escribo la orden en la línea de comandos.
example.en: I type the instruction on the command line.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: commands; computer instructions
I take it; I gather; I understand (an inference)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Entiendo que can introduce a conclusion drawn from what has just been said, much like English “I take it that...” It need not mean that the speaker has received an explanation.

example.en: I take it you are not coming today.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: doorbell
works; functions

cardDefinitions.promptEs: intentar que + otra persona + acción en subjuntivo
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone tries to get another person to do something?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of intentar, then que, name the other person when needed, and put that person's action in its special non-factual form.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: That special form is called the subjunctive. It presents the later action as the goal of the attempt rather than an established fact: ordinary abre changes to abra, and ordinary viene changes to venga. If the same person both tries and acts, use intentar followed directly by the action verb in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form instead.

example.en: We try to get Pablo to arrive early.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use compañero de piso for a man and compañera de piso for a woman.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Compañero or compañera names the person sharing something, and de piso specifies the shared apartment. Make compañero or compañera match the person's gender; piso stays unchanged.

example.es: Mi compañero de piso trabaja de noche.
example.en: My roommate works at night.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone is locked out or left outside?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a matching form of quedarse followed by fuera.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Quedarse describes ending up or remaining in a state, and fuera means outside. Context can make quedarse fuera mean being unable to enter, or “being locked out,” rather than merely choosing to stay outdoors. Match me, te, se, nos, os, or se and the form of quedar to the person and time.

example.es: Olvidé las llaves y me quedé fuera.
example.en: I forgot the keys and was locked out.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone leaves or causes a thing to remain in a certain state?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of dejar, name or replace the affected thing, then add the words that describe its resulting state.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Dejar changes for the person and time. The object is the person or thing affected, and the final description tells the state it remains in. If that description is an adjective, it matches the object: dejé la puerta abierta but dejé los cajones abiertos.

example.en: They left the kitchen clean.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use línea de comandos.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This is the conventional computing term for a text interface where a person types commands instead of choosing controls in a graphical interface. Línea stays singular, while comandos is normally plural.

example.es: Abro el programa desde la línea de comandos.
example.en: I open the program from the command line.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say “turn the volume up”?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a matching form of subir followed by el volumen.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Subir can mean that something goes up or that someone raises it. With el volumen as its object, it conventionally means increasing the sound level. Change subir for the person and time; el volumen stays the same.

example.en: Can you turn the volume up?

cardDefinitions.promptEs: OS X · say · sintetizador de voz por línea de comandos
cardDefinitions.questionEn: What makes it possible for a Mac to speak text from the command line?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: OS X includes a command named say that sends typed text to the system speech synthesizer.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: A terminal command is text entered into a command-line interface. Running say followed by words makes the Mac read those words aloud; command-line tools can also adjust settings such as volume. The joke depends on remote access to the Mac and this built-in speech tool.

No stays before the completed verb phrase because nada follows it; both negatives reinforce one negative meaning in Spanish.
Para introduces the intended purpose, and tirarle stays in its unchanged -ar form with le attached.
Le attaches to the unchanged verb tirar and marks the person affected by what happens to the item named afterward.
Here the attached le points to the female roommate as the person affected.
Because le has already identified the female roommate, la introduces the feminine item associated with her.
The le attached to tirar identifies the affected owner, while la agrees with the feminine item ventana; natural English expresses that relationship with a possessive.

applications.explanationEn: Dejé names the completed action, el volumen fills the affected-object slot, and muy bajo states the low level left in place.
Así and que combine to introduce the next action as a result.
Estoy matches the speaker, and leyendo uses -iendo to present the reading as in progress.
Me adds the sense of working through the specified reading, while estoy leyendo supplies the matching ongoing form.
Para introduces the purpose, and averiguar stays in its unchanged -ar form.
Cómo keeps its written accent because it asks for the unknown method, and subir follows in its unchanged -ir form.

applications.exampleEs: CÓMO SUBIR EL VOLUMEN POR LÍNEA DE COMANDOS
applications.explanationEn: Cómo introduces the unknown method inside a larger statement, so it keeps its written accent even without question marks around this clause.
Subir supplies the increase action, and el volumen names the sound level being raised.
Línea names the text interface, and de comandos specifies that it accepts computer commands.
